title: What is binary search — find an element in a SORTED array by checking the middle; if target is smaller go left, if bigger go right; O(log n) — much faster than linear search.

s1_definition.profdef: Binary search is an efficient algorithm for finding a target in a sorted array by repeatedly halving the search range. It examines the middle element; if it matches, the search ends; if the target is smaller, it discards the right half; if larger, it discards the left half. Each comparison eliminates half the remaining elements, giving logarithmic time complexity. The precondition is strict: the data must be sorted.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine looking up an account in the National Bank of India's register, which is sorted by account number. Instead of reading from page one, you open the book right in the middle. If the account you want is smaller than the middle one, you know it is in the first half, so you ignore the second half entirely and open the middle of the first half. You keep halving the book, and within a handful of jumps you land on the exact page. Compared to flipping every page, this is dramatically faster.
s1_definition.oneliner: Binary search halves a sorted range at each step, finding the target in logarithmic time.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Binary search is an efficient algorithm for finding a target in a sorted array by repeatedly halving the search range. It examines the middle element; if it matches, the search ends; if the target is smaller, it discards the right half; if larger, it discards the left half. Each comparison eliminates half the remaining elements, giving logarithmic time complexity. The precondition is strict: the data must be sorted.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine looking up an account in the National Bank of India's register, which is sorted by account number. Instead of reading from page one, you open the book right in the middle. If the account you want is smaller than the middle one, you know it is in the first half, so you ignore the second half entirely and open the middle of the first half. You keep halving the book, and within a handful of jumps you land on the exact page. Compared to flipping every page, this is dramatically faster.

**One line to remember:** Binary search halves a sorted range at each step, finding the target in logarithmic time.

sections.s2_technical:
Binary search maintains two pointers, low and high, that bound the current search range. It computes the middle index and compares the middle element to the target, then narrows the range to one half.

The middle index must be computed safely. Writing `int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;` instead of `(low + high) / 2` avoids integer overflow when low and high are both large, a classic bug that broke binary search implementations for years. The comparison drives the narrowing: `if (arr[mid].compareTo(target) == 0) return mid;` is a hit, `else if (arr[mid].compareTo(target) < 0) low = mid + 1;` discards the left half including mid, and `else high = mid - 1;` discards the right half. The loop continues while low is less than or equal to high, and if the pointers cross without a match the target is absent.

The power is the halving. With a million elements, linear search may need a million comparisons, but binary search needs at most about twenty, because each step halves the range. In general it is log base two of n comparisons. The non-negotiable precondition is that the array is sorted; on unsorted data binary search gives wrong answers.

A senior-level point is that binary search generalises far beyond finding an exact value. It finds the insertion point for a new element, the first or last occurrence of a duplicate, or the boundary in a monotonic predicate, which is the basis of binary-search-on-the-answer problems. Java provides `Arrays.binarySearch` and `Collections.binarySearch`, both requiring sorted input, and TreeMap's floor and ceiling methods are binary search in disguise. In banking, this underpins fast lookups in sorted ledgers and range queries.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India keeps a sorted array of account numbers for a branch and must answer, thousands of times per second, whether a given account number exists and where. Scanning the whole array for each query is wasteful when the data is already sorted. Binary search jumps to the middle and halves the range each step, finding the account in a handful of comparisons.

Problem 2 — When an account is not found, the system still needs to respond quickly and clearly rather than scanning to the end. Binary search detects absence the moment its pointers cross, so a missing account is reported just as fast as a present one.

In our mini-project we build an `AccountLookup` that performs iterative binary search over a sorted array of account numbers, returning the index or minus one. The demo searches for a present and an absent account and logs each halving step so the logarithmic shrinking is visible.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: the sorted array of six accounts, searching for SAV4002 then SAV9999.

Step 1: For SAV4002, low is zero and high is five. The middle index is two, holding SAV3050. SAV3050 is smaller than SAV4002, so we discard the left half and set low to three.

Step 2: Now low is three and high is five. The middle index is four, holding SAV5003. SAV5003 is larger than SAV4002, so we discard the right half and set high to three.

Step 3: Now low is three and high is three. The middle index is three, holding SAV4002. It matches, so we return index three. Only three comparisons were needed for six elements.

Step 4: For SAV9999, low is zero and high is five. Middle index two is SAV3050, smaller, so low becomes three.

Step 5: Low three, high five, middle index four is SAV5003, smaller than SAV9999, so low becomes five. Low five, high five, middle index five is SAV6004, smaller, so low becomes six.

Step 6: Now low is six and high is five, so low exceeds high and the loop ends. The target was never found, so we return minus one, detecting absence quickly without scanning further.

```

[2026-10-26 20:55:02] INFO      range [3..5], mid=4 (SAV5003)
[2026-10-26 20:55:02] INFO      range [3..3], mid=3 (SAV4002)

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  sorted: [SAV1000, SAV2001, SAV3050, SAV4002, SAV5003, SAV6004]
            0        1        2        3        4        5

  search SAV4002:
    [0..5] mid=2 SAV3050 < target → low=3
    [3..5] mid=4 SAV5003 > target → high=3
    [3..3] mid=3 SAV4002 = target → FOUND at 3

  each step halves the range: 6 → 3 → 1 element
```

  └───────────────────────────────────────┘
      Pre:  array sorted ascending (non-negotiable)
      Post: returns index if present else -1

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────

  1. low=0, high=n-1
  2. while low<=high: mid=low+(high-low)/2
  3. compare; narrow low or high; return mid on match
  4. crossed → return -1
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Binary search is an efficient algorithm for finding a target in a sorted array by repeatedly halving the search range. I keep two pointers, low and high, that bound the current range. I look at the middle element: if it matches the target I am done, if the target is smaller I discard the right half, and if it is larger I discard the left half. Because every comparison eliminates half of the remaining elements, binary search runs in logarithmic time, which is dramatically faster than the linear scan it replaces.

The non-negotiable precondition I always state up front is that the data must be sorted. On unsorted data binary search simply gives wrong answers. I also always compute the midpoint as low plus high minus low over two rather than low plus high over two, because the naive form can overflow when the indices are large, which is a famous bug that lurked in standard libraries for years.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used binary search over a sorted array of account numbers for a branch, where we answer existence-and-location queries thousands of times per second. With a million accounts a linear scan could take a million comparisons, but binary search needs only about twenty, and it detects a missing account just as fast, the moment the pointers cross, so absence is reported without scanning to the end.

The senior-level point I add is that binary search generalises far beyond exact matching. The same halving idea finds the insertion point for a new element, the first or last occurrence among duplicates, or the boundary of a monotonic condition, which is the basis of binary-search-on-the-answer problems. Java gives me Arrays.binarySearch and Collections.binarySearch, both needing sorted input, and TreeMap's floor and ceiling are binary search underneath. In databases the same principle powers B-tree index lookups, so understanding binary search explains why a sorted index makes queries fast.
